\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation---or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
This makes both the validity and the regime-dependence of existing canary claims open questions with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.

We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across eight contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response (including a synchronous dip at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$) through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
The discovery is enabled by a multi-method consensus framework (MMCT)~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} comparing five statistical methods, which reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null---the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions spanning the full spectrum.
Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$ generations, canary-downstream causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, steepness $k{\geq}200$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent by power theory, Contribution~2): PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (dual-seed), despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
    A non-monotonic dose-response establishes a four-regime structure: \emph{blind} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, PermG 0/8; sub-threshold signal present, see Contribution~2), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8, dual-seed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
    The detection threshold is governed by per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha$, not cumulative contamination.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed (distinct-1 drops 39.6\%) but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null (entropy drift $-5.3\%$ vs.\ null $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
    Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%), with directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) confirmed across four seeds on WikiText-103.

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A $S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha)$ framework predicts the non-monotonic dose-response: signal strength $S$ increases monotonically with $\alpha$, but temporal resolution $R$ drops at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$ when relaxation time matches the observation interval.
    A statistical power interpretation formalizes the onset as a power threshold---$\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma\bigr)$---generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$: left-shift of $\alpha_c$, transition smoothing, and method-dependent detection thresholds.
    Empirical validation of prediction~(iii) awaits $T{=}20$ replication; at $T{=}10$, sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}, \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
    The Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT), comparing five lead-lag methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, serves as the instrument enabling the above discovery.
    It exposes three methodological pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% (inter-method $\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 20/24 FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
    PermG emerges as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity, identifying token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection and cessation} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    Predictive cessation (triggered when token entropy drops ${>}15\%$) fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% (pooled estimate; bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%)\footnote{Bootstrap CI computed from two seed-precision pairs (s42 fp32, s43 bf16); the interval reflects observed variation rather than population-level uncertainty.} and enabling convergence one generation faster.
    A four-layer detection taxonomy---dimensionality collapse ($\alpha{\geq}0.10$), distributional variance ($\alpha{\geq}0.25$), causal coupling ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$), dynamical stability ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$)---provides practitioners with regime-appropriate diagnostic tools.
    Results are validated across two model scales (Pythia-410M, Pythia-1.4B), confirming scale-independent trigger and recovery patterns.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}), cross-architecture generalization (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), and canary-based early intervention (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and future directions, and \S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

2	\label{sec:experiments}

4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
27	Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
28	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all six contamination levels.

50	\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
51	\label{sec:method_sensitivity}
52	
53	We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
54	If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.
55	
56	\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
57	We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
58	The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{5/16} (31.3\%; moderate supplementary, \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
59	Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 37.5\%} among the primary methods: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
60	The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is at least \textbf{62.5\%} across the primary methods.
61	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.
62	
63	\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
64	A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
65	For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
66	For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
67	The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
68	Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.
69	
70	\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
71	Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
72	After correcting the statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$; however, the qualitative finding that this single hyperparameter can swing conclusions between near-universal significance and near-universal non-significance remains, consistent with known properties of the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
73	
74	\begin{figure}[t]
75	\centering
76	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
77	\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$; after correcting the implementation (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$, but the qualitative sensitivity to this hyperparameter persists.}
78	\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
79	\end{figure}
80	
81	\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
82	Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
83	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
84	Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation, which anchors the permissive extreme, and Toda--Yamamoto, which provides moderate supplementary signal) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
85	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
86	Direction checking (D111) itself constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: restricting to forward-direction associations inverts naive cross-correlation's profile from uniformly high (${\approx}100\%$ undirected) to regime-dependent, revealing that much of its apparent signal was reverse-directional.
87	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control), naive cross-correlation still finds \textbf{75\%} (6/8) of forward-direction pairs significant---lower than the undirected 100\%, but still a substantial FPR.
88	Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\%, achieving perfect null-control specificity.
89	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8), while naive finds 37.5\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}; Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
90	
91	\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
92	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that direction checking reshapes the method hierarchy across contamination levels.
93	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, naive cross-correlation drops to 12.5\% while permutation Granger remains at 0\%, narrowing the gap visible in undirected analysis.
94	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, naive rises to 87.5\% while permutation Granger reaches 75\%; both methods detect, but naive's persistent 75\% null-control FPR means its high-$\alpha$ detections cannot be distinguished from false positives without the consensus framework.
95	This regime-dependent reversal, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
96	
97	\paragraph{Why permutation Granger succeeds.}
98	The systematic comparison identifies PermG as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across all regimes where signal exists ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$).
99	Three properties explain this outcome.
100	First, the nonparametric permutation procedure inherently controls FPR by constructing the null distribution from the observed data rather than from distributional assumptions, making it robust to the non-stationarity that inflates false positives in correlation-based methods.
101	Second, Granger tests are directional by construction: they test whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history, naturally filtering the reverse-directional associations that inflate naive cross-correlation's FPR.
102	Third, PermG does not require threshold calibration or augmentation order selection, avoiding the hyperparameter sensitivity observed in Toda--Yamamoto (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}) and the power limitations that reduce threshold onset to near-zero detection under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}).
103	By contrast, differenced cross-correlation retains 100\% FDR significance in both forward \emph{and} reverse directions at $\alpha{=}0.75$, failing to distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics; and Toda--Yamamoto, while achieving moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
104	These complementary failures, exposed through the MMCT evaluation framework, converge on a single recommendation: for short iterative training series ($T{\leq}20$), permutation Granger causality should be the primary detection method.
105

132	\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
133	\label{sec:regime}
134	
135	Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
136	We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.
137	
138	\paragraph{Raw drift.}
139	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
140	Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
141	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
142	Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
143	At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
144	The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

156	\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
157	Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
158	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (including $\alpha{=}0.25$ where a faint single-pair signal appears at FDR $p{=}0.053$ but aggregate detection remains null, and $\alpha{=}0.35$/$0.40$/$0.45$ which confirm PermG fwd${=}$0/8), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), \textbf{3/8} and \textbf{0/8} at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (s42 and s43 respectively; dual-seed confirmed non-monotonic dip), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
159	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
160	Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
161	Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
162	Permutation Granger forward significance is the primary detection indicator (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): it reaches 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, dips to 3/8 at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (synchronous collapse zone; see below), and recovers to 5--6/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.

191	\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
192	Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
193	The transition from sub-threshold to reliably detectable occurs between $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: finer-grained probing confirms PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$, while $\alpha{=}0.50$ achieves 6/8 (2~seeds).
194	A faint single-pair signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (entropy$\to$distinct-1: raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), but all aggregate indicators remain null through $\alpha{=}0.45$, placing the onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$.
195	At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
196	Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.
197	
198	\paragraph{Quantifying the onset boundary.}
199	Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies the sharp onset observed above.
200	Fitting $P(\alpha) = 1/(1 + \exp(-k(\alpha - \alpha_c)))$ to the PermG forward detection rate yields a critical threshold $\alpha_c = 0.476$ with steepness $k \geq 200$ and transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
201	The sigmoid model explains 96.9\% of variance ($R^2 = 0.969$), substantially outperforming a power-law alternative ($R^2 = 0.808$; $\Delta\text{AIC} = 18.2$), confirming that the onset is steep rather than gradual.
202	This transition is striking because effective contamination barely changes across the boundary: after 10 generations of iterative training, both $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$ drive the cumulative synthetic fraction above 99\% ($C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$: $99.75\%$ vs.\ $99.90\%$)---a difference of 0.15 percentage points---yet causal detectability jumps from 0/8 to 6/8.
203	We term this a \emph{detection phase transition}: causal coupling emerges abruptly at a critical contamination threshold ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$) rather than scaling smoothly with contamination dose.
204	Within the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}), $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ localizes the point at which signal strength $S(\alpha)$ first crosses the detection floor, while the high steepness ($k \geq 200$) indicates that temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ remains large at onset---the entropy--diversity lag has not yet begun to compress.
205	Cross-architecture comparison reveals no monotonic relationship between model scale and onset sensitivity (Qwen-0.8B $\approx$ Pythia-6.9B $>$ Pythia-410M $>$ Pythia-1.4B $>$ SmolLM3-3B), suggesting that architecture and pre-training data exert stronger influence than parameter count on detection onset.

217	\paragraph{Specification curve robustness.}
218	To verify that the detection phase transition is not an artifact of analytical choices, we conduct a specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications across 29 experimental conditions.
219	Specifications vary lag order, differencing strategy, significance threshold, FDR correction method, and permutation count.
220	PermG maintains a 0\% false-positive rate at the null ($\alpha{=}0.00$) across all 1{,}160 specifications, while naive cross-correlation reaches 100\% regardless of specification---confirming that the FPR separation between methods is robust to analytical degrees of freedom.
221	The phase transition itself is specification-invariant: PermG detection rate remains near zero below $\alpha{=}0.50$ (${\sim}0\%$), rises to 81.2\% at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and reaches 87.5\% at $\alpha{=}0.75$ across all specifications.
222	This demonstrates that the onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ is a property of the data-generating process, not a consequence of researcher degrees of freedom in method configuration.
223	
224	\paragraph{Non-monotonic dose-response: the synchronous collapse zone.}
225	Dual-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reveals a non-monotonic dose-response in Granger detectability: PermG fwd drops to 3/8 (s42) and 0/8 (s43), below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds) and $\alpha{=}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, 3~seeds).
226	This creates a four-regime structure in the dose-response profile: \emph{blind} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, 0/8), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed; 6/8 at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
227	The dip confirms the non-monotonic prediction of the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): at $\alpha{=}0.60$, signal strength $S$ continues rising but temporal resolution $R$ drops sharply due to relaxation time matching, producing a local minimum in detectability.
228	The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind spot, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
229	Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection across this range (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with its detection at $\alpha{=}0.60$ suggesting partial inter-method complementarity in the synchronous collapse zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8.
230	This non-monotonicity also implies that simple threshold-based triggers (such as the 15\% entropy criterion in \S\ref{sec:intervention}) may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.
231	
232	\paragraph{Predictions for longer generation chains.}
233	The statistical power interpretation (\S\ref{sec:theory}) generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$.
234	Since $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S(\alpha) \cdot R(\alpha) \cdot \sqrt{T} \,/\, \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, increasing $T$ raises power at every $\alpha$:
235	(i)~$\alpha_c$ should \emph{left-shift}---the detection threshold decreases because $\sqrt{20}/\sqrt{10} \approx 1.41$ multiplies the power argument uniformly, so contamination levels currently below threshold (e.g., $\alpha{=}0.45$, where $T{=}10$ yields PermG 0/8 with sub-threshold $p$-values of 0.059--0.091) may cross into detectability;
236	(ii)~the transition should \emph{smooth}---the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling broadens the power curve across $\alpha$, making the onset less step-like (the synchronous dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ should also attenuate as finer temporal sampling resolves sub-generation lags);
237	(iii)~different methods should exhibit \emph{different} $\alpha_c$ values, since each method has its own power curve---empirical validation of this prediction awaits $T{=}20$ replication.
238	These predictions are currently under empirical verification with extended ($T{=}20$) generation protocols.

241	\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
242	\label{sec:case_study}
243	
244	Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
245	We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
246	
247	\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
248	Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

261	\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}

263	However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
264	Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

266	\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
267	ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
268	Across 7 validated conditions at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent with unidirectional forward causation at full synthetic replacement; domain-dependent bidirectionality emerges at lower $\alpha$, \S\ref{sec:discussion}), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
269	This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
270	This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.

274	Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
275	Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
276	The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
277	This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

279	\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}

281	The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:method_sensitivity}

We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.

\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{5/16} (31.3\%; moderate supplementary, \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 37.5\%} among the primary methods: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is at least \textbf{62.5\%} across the primary methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.

\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.

\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
After correcting the statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$; however, the qualitative finding that this single hyperparameter can swing conclusions between near-universal significance and near-universal non-significance remains, consistent with known properties of the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical}.

\centering

\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$; after correcting the implementation (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$, but the qualitative sensitivity to this hyperparameter persists.}
\label{fig:differencing_dmax}

\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation, which anchors the permissive extreme, and Toda--Yamamoto, which provides moderate supplementary signal) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
Direction checking (D111) itself constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: restricting to forward-direction associations inverts naive cross-correlation's profile from uniformly high (${\approx}100\%$ undirected) to regime-dependent, revealing that much of its apparent signal was reverse-directional.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control), naive cross-correlation still finds \textbf{75\%} (6/8) of forward-direction pairs significant---lower than the undirected 100\%, but still a substantial FPR.
Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\%, achieving perfect null-control specificity.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8), while naive finds 37.5\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}; Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that direction checking reshapes the method hierarchy across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, naive cross-correlation drops to 12.5\% while permutation Granger remains at 0\%, narrowing the gap visible in undirected analysis.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, naive rises to 87.5\% while permutation Granger reaches 75\%; both methods detect, but naive's persistent 75\% null-control FPR means its high-$\alpha$ detections cannot be distinguished from false positives without the consensus framework.
This regime-dependent reversal, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.

\paragraph{Why permutation Granger succeeds.}
The systematic comparison identifies PermG as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across all regimes where signal exists ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$).
Three properties explain this outcome.
First, the nonparametric permutation procedure inherently controls FPR by constructing the null distribution from the observed data rather than from distributional assumptions, making it robust to the non-stationarity that inflates false positives in correlation-based methods.
Second, Granger tests are directional by construction: they test whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history, naturally filtering the reverse-directional associations that inflate naive cross-correlation's FPR.
Third, PermG does not require threshold calibration or augmentation order selection, avoiding the hyperparameter sensitivity observed in Toda--Yamamoto (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}) and the power limitations that reduce threshold onset to near-zero detection under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}).
By contrast, differenced cross-correlation retains 100\% FDR significance in both forward \emph{and} reverse directions at $\alpha{=}0.75$, failing to distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics; and Toda--Yamamoto, while achieving moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
These complementary failures, exposed through the MMCT evaluation framework, converge on a single recommendation: for short iterative training series ($T{\leq}20$), permutation Granger causality should be the primary detection method.

\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
\label{sec:regime}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.

\paragraph{Raw drift.}
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (including $\alpha{=}0.25$ where a faint single-pair signal appears at FDR $p{=}0.053$ but aggregate detection remains null, and $\alpha{=}0.35$/$0.40$/$0.45$ which confirm PermG fwd${=}$0/8), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), \textbf{3/8} and \textbf{0/8} at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (s42 and s43 respectively; dual-seed confirmed non-monotonic dip), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
Permutation Granger forward significance is the primary detection indicator (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): it reaches 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, dips to 3/8 at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (synchronous collapse zone; see below), and recovers to 5--6/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$: finer-grained probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ yields PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at all three levels, extending the blind spot through $\alpha{=}0.45$.
A faint signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (best-pair FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not translate to aggregate detection; reliable detection begins at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds).
This steep onset is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ reveal sub-threshold signal: the minimum FDR-corrected $p$ reaches 0.059 (seed~43, 18\% above the $q{=}0.05$ threshold) and 0.091 (seed~42; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
This gradient is consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach significance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.

\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
The transition from sub-threshold to reliably detectable occurs between $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: finer-grained probing confirms PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$, while $\alpha{=}0.50$ achieves 6/8 (2~seeds).
A faint single-pair signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (entropy$\to$distinct-1: raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), but all aggregate indicators remain null through $\alpha{=}0.45$, placing the onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.

\paragraph{Quantifying the onset boundary.}
Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies the sharp onset observed above.
Fitting $P(\alpha) = 1/(1 + \exp(-k(\alpha - \alpha_c)))$ to the PermG forward detection rate yields a critical threshold $\alpha_c = 0.476$ with steepness $k \geq 200$ and transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
The sigmoid model explains 96.9\% of variance ($R^2 = 0.969$), substantially outperforming a power-law alternative ($R^2 = 0.808$; $\Delta\text{AIC} = 18.2$), confirming that the onset is steep rather than gradual.
This transition is striking because effective contamination barely changes across the boundary: after 10 generations of iterative training, both $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$ drive the cumulative synthetic fraction above 99\% ($C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$: $99.75\%$ vs.\ $99.90\%$)---a difference of 0.15 percentage points---yet causal detectability jumps from 0/8 to 6/8.
We term this a \emph{detection phase transition}: causal coupling emerges abruptly at a critical contamination threshold ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$) rather than scaling smoothly with contamination dose.
Within the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}), $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ localizes the point at which signal strength $S(\alpha)$ first crosses the detection floor, while the high steepness ($k \geq 200$) indicates that temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ remains large at onset---the entropy--diversity lag has not yet begun to compress.
Cross-architecture comparison reveals no monotonic relationship between model scale and onset sensitivity (Qwen-0.8B $\approx$ Pythia-6.9B $>$ Pythia-410M $>$ Pythia-1.4B $>$ SmolLM3-3B), suggesting that architecture and pre-training data exert stronger influence than parameter count on detection onset.

\paragraph{Specification curve robustness.}
To verify that the detection phase transition is not an artifact of analytical choices, we conduct a specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications across 29 experimental conditions.
Specifications vary lag order, differencing strategy, significance threshold, FDR correction method, and permutation count.
PermG maintains a 0\% false-positive rate at the null ($\alpha{=}0.00$) across all 1{,}160 specifications, while naive cross-correlation reaches 100\% regardless of specification---confirming that the FPR separation between methods is robust to analytical degrees of freedom.
The phase transition itself is specification-invariant: PermG detection rate remains near zero below $\alpha{=}0.50$ (${\sim}0\%$), rises to 81.2\% at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and reaches 87.5\% at $\alpha{=}0.75$ across all specifications.
This demonstrates that the onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ is a property of the data-generating process, not a consequence of researcher degrees of freedom in method configuration.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic dose-response: the synchronous collapse zone.}
Dual-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reveals a non-monotonic dose-response in Granger detectability: PermG fwd drops to 3/8 (s42) and 0/8 (s43), below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds) and $\alpha{=}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, 3~seeds).
This creates a four-regime structure in the dose-response profile: \emph{blind} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, 0/8), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed; 6/8 at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
The dip confirms the non-monotonic prediction of the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): at $\alpha{=}0.60$, signal strength $S$ continues rising but temporal resolution $R$ drops sharply due to relaxation time matching, producing a local minimum in detectability.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind spot, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection across this range (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with its detection at $\alpha{=}0.60$ suggesting partial inter-method complementarity in the synchronous collapse zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8.
This non-monotonicity also implies that simple threshold-based triggers (such as the 15\% entropy criterion in \S\ref{sec:intervention}) may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.

\paragraph{Predictions for longer generation chains.}
The statistical power interpretation (\S\ref{sec:theory}) generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$.
Since $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S(\alpha) \cdot R(\alpha) \cdot \sqrt{T} \,/\, \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, increasing $T$ raises power at every $\alpha$:
(i)~$\alpha_c$ should \emph{left-shift}---the detection threshold decreases because $\sqrt{20}/\sqrt{10} \approx 1.41$ multiplies the power argument uniformly, so contamination levels currently below threshold (e.g., $\alpha{=}0.45$, where $T{=}10$ yields PermG 0/8 with sub-threshold $p$-values of 0.059--0.091) may cross into detectability;
(ii)~the transition should \emph{smooth}---the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling broadens the power curve across $\alpha$, making the onset less step-like (the synchronous dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ should also attenuate as finer temporal sampling resolves sub-generation lags);
(iii)~different methods should exhibit \emph{different} $\alpha_c$ values, since each method has its own power curve---empirical validation of this prediction awaits $T{=}20$ replication.
These predictions are currently under empirical verification with extended ($T{=}20$) generation protocols.


\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) on WikiText-103 find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing directional asymmetry in this domain.\footnote{C4 exhibits domain-dependent directionality: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 20/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
Across 7 validated conditions at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent with unidirectional forward causation at full synthetic replacement; domain-dependent bidirectionality emerges at lower $\alpha$, \S\ref{sec:discussion}), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline (PermG fwd ${\geq}6/8$, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 75\% forward-direction FPR to 0\%, matching the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).

\label{sec:smollm3}
SmolLM3-3B (PermG fwd 3/8) reveals that canary metric choice is itself a dimension of method sensitivity.
Decomposing by canary type: ECE$\to$downstream achieves 3/4 significant pairs, while token entropy$\to$downstream achieves 0/4.

\label{sec:intervention}

To test whether the lead-lag relationship translates into practical utility, we implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ is switched to $0.0$ (pure real data).
We compare against a reactive baseline that triggers only when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$---a downstream metric that, by the lead-lag hypothesis, should respond later.

Predictive intervention reduces peak perplexity by 63\% relative to reactive ($56.99$ vs.\ $157.09$, s42 fp32) and achieves full recovery by generation~2 versus generation~4 for reactive.
The bf16 pair shows a milder perturbation (peak perplexity $24.65$ vs.\ $56.99$) consistent with stochastic rounding regularization, but the structural pattern---generation~1 trigger, generation~2 recovery---is identical.
Both conditions converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

\paragraph{Cross-scale validation: Pythia-1.4B.}
Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32) replicates the 410M pattern: token entropy drops $51.9\%$ at generation~1 ($2.946{\to}1.418$), exceeding the 15\% threshold, and recovers to $2.892$ by generation~2 ($98.2\%$ of baseline).
Perplexity spikes from $19.68$ to $65.37$ at the trigger generation and recovers to $17.44$ by generation~2 (stable at $17.60$ through generation~10).
The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap (410M to 1.4B), confirming that the canary-based intervention mechanism is scale-independent: the 15\% entropy threshold generalizes without recalibration across model sizes.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses (the current default) cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our systematic five-method comparison through the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) identifies permutation Granger causality as the recommended detection method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity, exhibiting a clean step-function dose-response from 0/8 (blind spot, $\alpha{\leq}0.45$) to 6/8 (onset, $\alpha{=}0.50$) with reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
The other four methods each fail in characteristic ways: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR to 75\%, differenced cross-correlation cannot separate forward from reverse precedence, threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}10$ under $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) as a supplementary method.

Applying permutation Granger, token entropy exhibits robust one-generation-ahead precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ on WikiText-103 (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 4~seeds, replicated on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B), with cross-architecture validation confirming detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 of 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B).
Directional asymmetry is domain-dependent: consistent unidirectionality holds on WikiText across all regimes, while C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8), though forward detection remains robust in both domains.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The methodological pitfalls we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series.

A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response (including a synchronous dip at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$) through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
The discovery is enabled by a multi-method consensus framework (MMCT)~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} comparing five statistical methods, which reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null---the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions spanning the full spectrum.
Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$ generations, canary-downstream causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, steepness $k{\geq}200$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent by power theory, Contribution~2): PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (dual-seed), despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
    A non-monotonic dose-response establishes a four-regime structure: \emph{blind} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, PermG 0/8; sub-threshold signal present, see Contribution~2), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8, dual-seed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
    The detection threshold is governed by per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha$, not cumulative contamination.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed (distinct-1 drops 39.6\%) but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null (entropy drift $-5.3\%$ vs.\ null $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
    Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%), with directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) confirmed across four seeds on WikiText-103.

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A $S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha)$ framework predicts the non-monotonic dose-response: signal strength $S$ increases monotonically with $\alpha$, but temporal resolution $R$ drops at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$ when relaxation time matches the observation interval.
    A statistical power interpretation formalizes the onset as a power threshold---$\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma\bigr)$---generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$: left-shift of $\alpha_c$, transition smoothing, and method-dependent detection thresholds.

26

28	
29	- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证

32	- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing
33	
34	### 1.2 主线统一性
35	
36	- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
37	- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
38	- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机

40	
41	### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义
42	
43	- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
44	- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）

47

49	
50	- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
51	- 重点学：
52	  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
53	  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
54	  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
55	  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
56	- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
57	- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文
58	
59	---
60	
61	## 二、Abstract 写作规范
62	
63	### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）
64	
65	Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：
66	1. **研究什么问题** — 1-2 句话交代背景和痛点
67	2. **为什么重要** — 现有方法的不足（不用写太多）
68	3. **本文提出什么** — 核心贡献的关键机制（简要，不堆砌细节）
69	4. **结果说明什么** — 用具体实验结论支撑贡献
70	
71	### 2.2 禁忌
72	
73	- **禁止堆砌数据**：Abstract 不是 Results 的缩写。最多引用 2-3 个关键数字，要服务于 claim
74	- **禁止过度宣传**：不说 "revolutionary"、"groundbreaking"
75	- **禁止写成 Introduction 的缩写**：Abstract 是独立阅读单元
76	- **禁止术语堆积**：如果审稿人几十秒内判断不出价值，就失败了
77	- **缩写必须定义**：Abstract 中首次出现的缩写必须展开
78	
79	### 2.3 审稿人视角检验
80	
81	写完后用这个标准自检：审稿人能否在 30 秒内判断——
82	- 问题是否重要？
83	- 方法是否清楚？
84	- 贡献是否可信？
85	- 结果是否有说服力？
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 三、Introduction 写作规范
90	
91	### 3.1 完整叙事线（5 段结构）
92	
93	Introduction 需要从一个清晰、重要的问题切入，逐步把读者带到核心贡献：
94	
95	1. **研究背景**（1-2 段）：大模型在某类能力/应用中已取得进展，但仍存在一个关键瓶颈
96	2. **问题重要性**（1 段）：结合真实应用、已有方法局限或当前趋势，说明这不是小问题
97	3. **现有方法不足**（1 段）：系统梳理为什么不够（依赖更大模型/更多数据/更复杂推理/更高成本，或只在特定 benchmark 有效）
98	4. **本文核心想法**（1 段）：我们观察到什么、提出了什么方法、为什么能解决上述问题
99	5. **贡献总结**（列表）：清楚列出方法贡献、实验贡献和分析贡献
100	
101	### 3.2 整体叙事结构
102	
103	```
104	现有进展 → 关键缺口 → 本文洞察 → 方法概述 → 实验证据 → 贡献总结
105	```
106	
107	### 3.3 禁忌
108	
109	- **禁止泛泛介绍**：不要开头就写 "LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities..."，要从具体问题切入
110	- **禁止缺少过渡**：每段之间必须有逻辑连接
111	- **禁止实验报告风格**：Introduction 不是 "我们做了 X 实验得到了 Y 结果" 的罗列
112	- 每条 Contribution 必须有对应的 section/table 支撑
113	- Contribution 列表中不能出现未在前文铺垫过的概念
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 四、Related Work 写作规范
118	
119	### 4.1 目标
120	
121	让审稿人相信：作者理解这个领域，知道自己的方法站在什么位置，清楚相对已有工作的真实增量在哪里。
122	
123	### 4.2 结构要求
124	
125	- 把已有工作分成几个清晰的主题（如模型训练、推理增强、工具调用、数据构建、评测等）
126	- 每类简要说明：已有方法做了什么、解决了哪些问题、和本文的关系
127	- 帮助读者理解：哪些是本文直接继承的，哪些方法不同但解决相似问题，哪些留下了本文要解决的缺口
128	
129	### 4.3 禁忌
130	
131	- **禁止论文堆砌**：不要写成 "A proposed X. B proposed Y. C proposed Z." 的列表
132	- **目标不是展示读了多少论文**，而是做归纳和比较
133	- Contribution claim（"To our knowledge, no prior work..."）应放在 Introduction，不在 Related Work
134	
135	### 4.4 引用充足度
136	
137	- 引用必须覆盖：**直接相关方法、baseline 论文、评测 benchmark 论文、理论基础**
138	- 任何一类缺失，审稿人会立刻看出来调研不充分
139	- 引用密度参照目标会议近年录用论文的量级——明显偏少意味着 Related Work 调研不足
140	
141	---
142	
143	## 五、去 AI 写作风格（硬规则）
144	
145	以下模式是 AI 生成文本的典型标志，审稿人一眼能看出。**必须全部消除。**
146	
147	### 5.1 严禁破折号（最显著的 AI 痕迹）
148	
149	**这是 AI 写作最容易被识别的标志，审稿人最敏感。单列为最高优先级硬规则。**
150	
151	- 解释性 em-dash（—，U+2014）和 en-dash（–，U+2013）必须**全部删除**
152	- 替代方式：用逗号、括号或拆分为两个句子
153	- 强制检查命令：
154	  ```bash
155	  grep -n "—" paper/*.tex     # em-dash，每处人工判断是否必要
156	  grep -n " – " paper/*.tex   # 解释性 en-dash，几乎都应删除
157	  ```
158	- 例外（允许保留）：表格分隔符、数字范围（`2020–2024`、`pp. 12–18`）、专有名词（`Newton–Raphson`）
159	
160	### 5.2 段落与句式
161	
162	- **禁止过度分段**：不需要每 2-3 句就换段，自然段 5-8 句是正常的
163	- **减少关系从句**（which, that, who）：能用简洁直接的句子就不用从句
164	- **禁止 -ing 短语结尾**：如 "..., highlighting the applicability of..." / "..., demonstrating the effectiveness of..."。这是 AI 写作最典型的标志之一
165	- **禁止连续使用 "Furthermore" / "Moreover" / "Additionally"**：一段内最多用一个过渡词
166	- **避免 "It is worth noting that..." / "Notably, ..."**：直接写要说的内容
167	
168	### 5.3 用词黑名单
169	
170	- 避免 "delve into" / "leverage" / "utilize" / "facilitate" — 用 "explore" / "use" / "enable"
171	- 避免 "a myriad of" / "a plethora of" — 用 "many" / "various"
172	- 避免 "in the realm of" / "in the context of" — 直接说
173	- 避免 "paradigm shift" / "novel" 过度使用
174	
175	### 5.4 校对清单（4 步）
176	
177	1. 全文 proofread 语法和拼写
178	2. 检查所有代词/指示词（this, that, it）是否指代明确
179	3. **`grep "—"` + `grep " – "` 全文清零**（删除所有解释性 dash，§5.1）
180	4. `grep "ing,"` 模式——大部分 -ing 分词短语需要改写
181	
182	---
183	
184	## 六、图表与视觉规范
185	
186	### 6.1 知识密度原则
187	
188	- **图表的信息必须紧凑**——不能为了美观而留大量白空间
189	- 一张图如果只传达一个简单信息，要么缩小要么合并到其他图中
190	- 能用 inline text 说清的不要占一整个 Figure
191	
192	### 6.2 表格规范
193	
194	- 表格和正文文字不能视觉重叠（检查 column 宽度和 alignment）
195	- 小数精度全表统一
196	- 最优加粗、次优下划线
197	- Caption 必须自包含
198	
199	### 6.3 图片规范
200	
201	- 数值标签不能被线、bar、点遮住——用白色背景或偏移标签
202	- 图中字体 >= 7pt（打印后仍可读）
203	- 栏宽约束需匹配目标 venue 模板要求
204	- 概念图/流程图要有信息量，不要画一个 trivial 的 pipeline 然后占半页
205	
206	### 6.4 空间效率
207	
208	- 顶会正文页数严格受限（具体页数查目标会议官网），每 cm² 都是宝贵资源
209	- 优先使用 `\subfigure` 合并相关图
210	- Table 能 inline 就不要单独浮动
211	- 图表占比与其对叙事的贡献成正比
212	
213	### 6.5 页面节奏
214	
215	好论文的页面有节奏感——text、equation、figure 交替出现，读者视觉不疲劳：
216	
217	- **text-equation-figure 三重奏**：重要概念用"文字解释 → 公式定义 → 图表直觉"三步展开
218	- 连续 2 页纯文本（无 figure/equation/table）→ 穿插一个 display item 打破节奏
219	- 连续 2 个 figure 页（整页被 float 占满）→ 至少隔 1 段文字再放下一个 float
220	- Section heading 不孤悬页底（heading 后至少跟 2 行正文，否则强制分页）
221	- 最后一页内容 ≥ 2/3 页面高度（太空显得凑数，太满放不下 references）
222	
223	### 6.6 表格 LaTeX 规范
224	
225	**Booktabs 标准（硬规则）**：
226	- 用 `\toprule` / `\midrule` / `\bottomrule`，禁止 `\hline`，禁止竖线 `|`
227	- 用 `\centering` 不用 `\begin{center}`（后者多加垂直空白）
228	- 最优结果加粗（`\textbf{}`），次优下划线（`\underline{}`）+ 方向箭头 `↑`/`↓` 标明指标方向
229	- 小数精度全表统一（如全部保留 1 位或 2 位）
230	- Caption 在表格上方（`\caption` 在 `\begin{tabular}` 之前）
231	
232	**宽度决策树**：
233	- ≤5 列 → 单栏宽度（`\columnwidth`）
234	- 6–8 列 → 全文宽度（`\textwidth`，双栏模板用 `table*`）
235	- >8 列 → 拆成两张表或移入 appendix
236	
237	---
238	
239	## 七、投稿前通用准备
240	
241	### 7.1 模板必须官方（硬规则）
242	
243	- LaTeX 模板**必须从目标会议官网下载**（CallForPapers / Author Instructions 页面）
244	- **不要用**：
245	  - 网上他人转载的复制版本（可能被改过 margin / 行号设置）
246	  - 上一年的模板（参数可能变：字体、margin、行号、anonymous 选项等）
247	  - 组里学长留的旧版本（来源不明、无法追溯）
248	- 风险：
249	  - 样式不符合 → desk reject
250	  - margin 不对 → 被审稿人质疑诚信
251	  - reference 格式错 → 被认为不规范
252	- 流程：先查会议官网 templates → 找不到再 `WebSearch "{venue} {year} latex template official"` → 仍找不到汇报 Director（不要用就近年版本顶替）
253	- `\documentclass[]{}` 选项必须与目标 venue + 阶段（review / camera-ready）一致
254	
255	### 7.2 投稿要求逐项核对
256	
257	- 目标会议如要求 Checklist / Ethical Statement / Broader Impact Statement / Reproducibility Statement，必须**认真填每一项**，不要全写 N/A
258	- 页数限制：查目标会议官网
259	- 匿名化要求：review 版 vs camera-ready 版本设置不同
260	- 行号开启（review 版常需）
261	- 字体大小、margin 不得修改 sty 文件
262	
263	### 7.3 最终修改 10 项检查流程
264	
265	提交前必须逐一检查：
266	1. 所有最新实验结果已全部录入
267	2. 根据实验结果将叙事调至最优状态
268	3. 附录所有内容在正文中被引用且融入叙事
269	4. 无数据堆砌（每个数字服务于叙事推进）
270	5. Abstract 和 Introduction 具有吸引力（不是实验报告风格）
271	6. 全文主线统一（idea 变化后各章节逻辑一致）
272	7. 所有专有名词有定义
273	8. 无 AI 风格标志（dash、-ing phrases、过度分段）
274	9. 图表知识密度高、无视觉遮挡
275	10. Reference 覆盖直接相关方法、baseline、benchmark、理论基础
276
